texts.preamble: M/S Buttercup Confectionary Ltd vs Food Safety Officer on 30 October, 2019 In The Court Of Sh. Yashwant Kumar District & Sessions Judge/Fsat: Patiala House Courts New Delhi In the matter of : Fsat No. 27/16 (Old Fsat No. 9/15) Cnr No. : Dlnd010012052015 M/s Buttercup Confectionary Ltd. R4, Inderpuri, New Delhi110 012 Through its Authorized person Sh. Upendra Kumar Mehto .... Appellant Versus Food Safety Officer Department of Food Safety Govt. of Delhi 8th Floor, Mayur Bhawan Connaught Place, New Delhi110001. ..... Respondent Appeal Against The Order Dated 03.06.2015 Of Ld. Adjudicating Officer, District Magistrate (New Delhi) Judgment
texts.facts: Vs FSO Page No. 1 of 17 selling substandard food as well as misbranding of the same, in violation of Section 26(2)(ii) & Section 27(1) r/w Section 3(1)(i) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 ("FSS Act" in short) and Regulation no.2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of the Food Safety & Standards (Packaging & Labelling) Regulations, 2011 ("FSS (P&L) Regulations" in short). 2. Facts in brief as per the appeal are that on 11.11.2012, Food Safety Officer ("FSO" in short), had taken the sample of "Chocolate", from the premises of M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd., Inderpuri, New Delhi, for analysis. The Food Analyst vide his report dated 26.11.2012 opined that the sample contains extraneous matter viz. added vegetable fats in contravention of Section 3(1) (i)of the FSS Act. He further opined that the sample was also found misbranded because there was violation of Regulation No. 2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of FSS (P&L) Regulation, 2011. The Food Safety Officer filed a complaint/application under Rule 3.1.1(3) FSS Rules, 2011 before the Ld. ADM alleging violation of Section 26(2) M/S Buttercup Confectionary Ltd vs Food Safety Officer on 30 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69080198/ 1 (ii), Section 27(1) read with Section 3(1)(i) of FSS Act and Regulation no.2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of FSS (P&L) Regulation, punishable under Sections 52 of FSS Act. Notice of the same was issued to the appellant and hearing was given. 4. The Ld. Chief PP for the respondent/State has not filed reply to the appeal, however, he has opposed the appeal.
texts.arguments: 3. The appellant has challenged the impugned order inter alia on the grounds among others that Ld. ADM failed to appreciate the evidence on record i.e. the Form VA wherein FSO not only wrongly M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors. Vs FSO Page No. 2 of 17 described the sample of "Fundoo Chocolate" as "Chocolate" but also illegally applied the standards of Milk Chocolate, which is different article of food. The "Fundoo Chocolate" is of the category of Filled Chocolates which contained confectionery in the centre distinct in composition from the outer covering Fundoo Chocolate, which was of Chocolate only. Ld. ADM failed to appreciate that the sanction of the case is bad in law as the Designated Officer did not accord sanction of Milk Chocolate to institute the prosecution against the appellant. The Food Analyst had no authority to change the nomenclature of food article. The Ld. ADM wrongly relied upon the contention of the Food Analyst that central and outer portion of the Fundoo Chocolate were not distinct as the Food Analyst had brought the package of remnants of the sample during crossexamination after long lapse of time, which were stored at room temperature and because of this, the central portion and outer portion of the Fundoo Chocolate had got diminished. It is well known that Chocolates cannot be properly stored at room temperature as it cannot retain its original shape at the room temperature and required to be stored at a temperature of 16 to 20 degree centigrade for proper storage. The Ld. ADM did not appreciate that on the notice of Form VA, the FSO had noted down the declaration as "contains added flavor". The only allegation against the company could be that label does not contain the name of flavor. The declaration of labeling regulations was not required as the packages were not of the category of pre packed packages. The Ld. ADM failed to appreciate that the word "Fundoo" M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors. Vs FSO Page No. 3 of 17 was not the brand name of the chocolate. The brand name was given on the packages as "Choco Swiss" and the same was also noted down by the Food Analyst in his report. 6. Ld. Counsel for the appellant argued that standards of chocolates have been defined in regulation 2.7.4. The sample article is not a standardized chocolate. The sampled article Fundoo Chocolate was tested illegally as Milk Chocolate and the Food Analyst had no authority to consider and treat the Fundoo chocolate as milk chocolate. The FSO is not authorized to change the nomenclature of the food article. The notification dt. 15.05.2017 of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare defines the types of chocolates. According to the Regulation 2.7.4 of the said notification, the addition of vegetable fats other than cocoa butter shall not exceed 5 percent of the finished product, after M/S Buttercup Confectionary Ltd vs Food Safety Officer on 30 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69080198/ 2 deduction of the total weight of any other added edible foodstuffs without reducing the minimum contents of cocoa materials. Ld. Counsel for the appellant further argued that new standards came in the year 2017 and the report of the FSO is prior to the year 2017, therefore, the respondent should have withdrawn its case against the appellant. The Ld. Counsel for the M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors. Vs FSO Page No. 4 of 17 appellant further argued that as per order dt.08.12.2017 issued by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, New Delhi, the Commissioners of Food Safety, were advised to withdraw, or, at least, not pursue, cases for violation of old norms and standards unless these are still not in conformity with the new/revised standards so that avoidable harassment of FBOs could be prevented. Form VA mentions that food articles contain added flavours. In the crossexamination of Food Analyst, he admitted that the sample received by him were not sealed but in a closed condition. Food Analyst further admitted in his crossexamination that the sample had been sealed by Cellotape, which was already there and it was not put by him. The cellotape may again be removed and in this regard, Ld. Counsel for the appellant placed reliance upon the judgment in the case of State of Kerala vs. K.S. Balakrishnan in Criminal Appeal No. 187/1972 decided on 13.09.1972 by the Hon'ble Kerala High Court. The sample had been taken from the manufacturing place. The packaging process was incomplete and the sample was taken forcibly. As per judgment in Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Nand Kishore, it is only when the process of manufacture is complete then it can be said that an article of food has been manufactured for sale. 7. Ld. Counsel for the appellant further argued that only Section 54 of the FSA is attracted in this case. As per the report of Food Analyst, the sample article contains extraneous matter, which is added vegetable fats. The report is being challenged. Ld. Counsel for the appellant referred the judgment in the case of Harish Chand vs. State M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors. Vs FSO Page No. 5 of 17 and stated that there may be instances where a manufacturer markets a new type of food which may not conform to any of the descriptions mentioned in the schedule of Prevention of Food Adulteration Act. Such marketing of a food, not so covered, cannot by itself be treated as illegal. Ld. Counsel for the appellant further argued that no evidence is there that the sample was sold in the market and it was not ready for sale. Packing & labelling comes under manufacturing unless it is completely stamped and packed. If product has been obtained from market, then it is finally produced. Ld. Counsel for the appellant has referred the judgment in the case of Municipal Corporation of Delhi versus Nand Kishore in Criminal Revision No. 158 of 1972 decided on 09.08.1972 by the Hon'ble Delhi High Court and stated that if a Food Inspector insists upon taking the sample of an article of food which is not ready for human consumption, then, it will not amount to a sale of an article of food within the meaning of section 2(v) or section 2 (xiii) of the Act. Whereas, the chocolates cannot be properly stored at a room temperature since the chocolates cannot retain their original shape at room temperature and are required to be kept / stored at temperature 16 degree centigrade to 20 degree centigrade for proper storage but the Adjudicating Officer wrongly relied upon the said contention of the Food Analyst. The only allegation against the company could be that the label does not contain the name of flavor. The Adjudicating Officer did not appreciate the argument that packages were not of the category of pre packed packages, so all the declaration as required by the Labeling Regulation was not required. The appellant also raised the ground in the appeal that packages produced by the Food Analyst at the time of cross examination were found only closed by Cellotapes, which could be removed and put again without tempering the package. 12. Section 26 of the FSS Act 2006 provides responsibilities of the Food Business Operator. Sub clause (2)(ii) of Section 26 the said Act provides that no Food Business Operator shall himself or by any person on his behalf manufacturer, store, sell or distribute any article of food which is misbranded or substandard or contains extraneous matter. M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors. Vs FSO Page No. 10 of 17 Section 26 of the FSS Act, 2006, seeks to provide for the responsibilities of the food business operator to ensure that the articles of food satisfy the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder at all stages of production, processing, import, distribution and sale within the businesses under his control. Subclause (2) provides that no food business operator shall himself or by any person on his behalf manufacturer, store, sell or distribute any article of food which is misbranded or substandard or contains extraneous matter or which is for the time being prohibited by the Food Authority or the Central Government or the State Government in the interest of public health. Section 3(1)(i) FSS Act provides that "In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, "extraneous matter" means any matter contained in an article of food which may be carried from the raw materials, packaging materials or process systems used for its manufacture or which is added to it, but such matter does not render such article of food unsafe. 14. Regulation no.2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of FSS (P&L) Regulations provides that "Declaration regarding Food Additives Extraneous addition of flavouring agents to be mentioned on the label Where an extraneous flavouring agent has been added to any article of food, there shall be written just beneath the list of ingredients on the label attached to any package of food so flavoured, a statement in capital letters as below : CONTAINS ADDED FLAVOUR (specify type M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors. Vs FSO Page No. 11 of 17 flavouring agent as per Regulation 3.1.10(1) of Food Safety and Standards (Food Product Standards and Food Additive) Regulation, 2011. 15. In this context, the case of Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan 2016 (1) FAC 561 is referred, thereby the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that "since the M/S Buttercup Confectionary Ltd vs Food Safety Officer on 30 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69080198/ 6 amendment was beneficial to the accused persons, it can be applied even with respect to earlier cases as well which are pending in the Court." The relevant para quoted in the said judgment of Nemi Chand (Supra), is reproduced as under : "3. Mr. Sushil Kumar Jain, learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant, submits that though the appellant has some prima facie case even on merits, he would be giving up the plea on merits and his only submission is about the sentence which has been imposed by the courts below. He has in this behalf, argued that there has been an amendment in the Act by the Central Amendment Act 34 of 1976 whereby Section 16A was added and under the said section, only a fine is leviable. He has drawn our attention to the judgment of this Court in 'T. Barai v. Henry Ah Hoe and Another' [1982 (2) FAC 362] [1983 (1) SCC 177] wherein this Court held that since the amendment was beneficial to the accused persons, it can be applied even with respect to earlier cases as well which are pending in the Court. In the said judgment, the Court held as under: "22. It is only retroactive criminal legislation that is prohibited under Article 20(1). The prohibition contained in Article 20(1) is that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence prohibits nor shall M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors. Vs FSO Page No. 13 of 17 he be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. The rule of beneficial construction requires that even ex post facto law of such a type should be applied to mitigate the rigour of the law. This finds support in the following passage from Crales on Statute Law, 7th Edn., at pp. 38889: "Every ex post facto law...." said Chase, J., in the American case of Calder v. Bull "must necessarily be retrospective, but every retrospective law is not an ex post facto law. Every law that takes away or impairs rights vested agreeably to existing laws is retrospective, and is generally unjust and may be oppressive; it is a good general rule that a law should have no retrospect, but in cases in which the laws may justly and for the benefit of the community and also of individuals relate to a time antecedent to their commencement: as statutes of oblivion or of pardon. They are certainly retrospective, and literally both concerning and after the facts committed. But I do not consider any law ex post facto within the prohibition that mollifies the rigour of the criminal law, M/S Buttercup Confectionary Ltd vs Food Safety Officer on 30 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69080198/ 7 but only those that create or aggravate the crime, or increase the punishment or change the rules of evidence for the purpose of conviction.... There is a great and apparent difference between making an unlawful act lawful and the making an innocent action criminal and punishing it as a crime." Accordingly, applying the ratio of T. Barai, (1983) 1 SCC 177, the impugned order dt.03.06.2015 of the Ld. ADM is modified on the aspect of substandard article by imposing a penalty of Rs.50,000/, which shall be deposited within 30 days from the date of this order before the Ld. ADM. 18.

Whereas, the chocolates cannot be properly stored at a room temperature since the chocolates cannot retain their original shape at room temperature and are required to be kept / stored at temperature 16 degree centigrade to 20 degree centigrade for proper storage but the Adjudicating Officer wrongly relied upon the said contention of the Food Analyst. The only allegation against the company could be that the label does not contain the name of flavor. The Adjudicating Officer did not appreciate the argument that packages were not of the category of pre packed packages, so all the declaration as required by the Labeling Regulation was not required. The appellant also raised the ground in the appeal that packages produced by the Food Analyst at the time of cross examination were found only closed by Cellotapes, which could be removed and put again without tempering the package.
texts.other_lawyer_arguments: 12. Section 26 of the FSS Act 2006 provides responsibilities of the Food Business Operator. Sub clause (2)(ii) of Section 26 the said Act provides that no Food Business Operator shall himself or by any person on his behalf manufacturer, store, sell or distribute any article of food which is misbranded or substandard or contains extraneous matter. M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors. Vs FSO Page No. 10 of 17 Section 26 of the FSS Act, 2006, seeks to provide for the responsibilities of the food business operator to ensure that the articles of food satisfy the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder at all stages of production, processing, import, distribution and sale within the businesses under his control. Subclause (2) provides that no food business operator shall himself or by any person on his behalf manufacturer, store, sell or distribute any article of food which is misbranded or substandard or contains extraneous matter or which is for the time being prohibited by the Food Authority or the Central Government or the State Government in the interest of public health. M/S Buttercup Confectionary Ltd vs Food Safety Officer on 30 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69080198/ 5 13. Section 3(1)(i) FSS Act provides that "In this Act, unless the context otherwise requires, "extraneous matter" means any matter contained in an article of food which may be carried from the raw materials, packaging materials or process systems used for its manufacture or which is added to it, but such matter does not render such article of food unsafe. 14. Regulation no.2.2.2.5(ii)(b) of FSS (P&L) Regulations provides that "Declaration regarding Food Additives Extraneous addition of flavouring agents to be mentioned on the label Where an extraneous flavouring agent has been added to any article of food, there shall be written just beneath the list of ingredients on the label attached to any package of food so flavoured, a statement in capital letters as below : CONTAINS ADDED FLAVOUR (specify type M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors. Vs FSO Page No. 11 of 17 flavouring agent as per Regulation 3.1.10(1) of Food Safety and Standards (Food Product Standards and Food Additive) Regulation, 2011. 15. In this context, the case of Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan 2016 (1) FAC 561 is referred, thereby the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that "since the M/S Buttercup Confectionary Ltd vs Food Safety Officer on 30 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69080198/ 6 amendment was beneficial to the accused persons, it can be applied even with respect to earlier cases as well which are pending in the Court." The relevant para quoted in the said judgment of Nemi Chand (Supra), is reproduced as under : "3. In the said judgment, the Court held as under: "22. It is only retroactive criminal legislation that is prohibited under Article 20(1). The prohibition contained in Article 20(1) is that no person shall be convicted of any offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence prohibits nor shall M/s Buttercup Confectionery Ltd & Ors. Vs FSO Page No. 13 of 17 he be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at the time of the commission of the offence. The rule of beneficial construction requires that even ex post facto law of such a type should be applied to mitigate the rigour of the law. This finds support in the following passage from Crales on Statute Law, 7th Edn., at pp. 38889: "Every ex post facto law...." said Chase, J., in the American case of Calder v. Bull "must necessarily be retrospective, but every retrospective law is not an ex post facto law. Every law that takes away or impairs rights vested agreeably to existing laws is retrospective, and is generally unjust and may be oppressive; it is a good general rule that a law should have no retrospect, but in cases in which the laws may justly and for the benefit of the community and also of individuals relate to a time antecedent to their commencement: as statutes of oblivion or of pardon. They are certainly retrospective, and literally both concerning and after the facts committed. But I do not consider any law ex post facto within the prohibition that mollifies the rigour of the criminal law, M/S Buttercup Confectionary Ltd vs Food Safety Officer on 30 October, 2019 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/69080198/ 7 but only those that create or aggravate the crime, or increase the punishment or change the rules of evidence for the purpose of conviction.... There is a great and apparent difference between making an unlawful act lawful and the making an innocent action criminal and punishing it as a crime." Accordingly, applying the ratio of T. Barai, (1983) 1 SCC 177, the impugned order dt.03.06.2015 of the Ld. ADM is modified on the aspect of substandard article by imposing a penalty of Rs.50,000/, which shall be deposited within 30 days from the date of this order before the Ld. ADM. 18.
